question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True—imperfect tagging plus winner's-curse effects in discovery samples necessarily pull PGS R2 below SNP h2, ~60%.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True—SNP heritability estimates from methods like GREML are frequently inflated by subtle population stratification or cryptic relatedness that aren't fully captured in real cohorts, while a PGS is tested strictly out-of-sample and therefore reflects a lower bound even before tagging or winner's-curse effects are considered. I'd put maybe 55% on this being the dominant reason in practice.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, 55%—LD-score finite-sample bias routinely inflates SNP h2 relative to PGS R2.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability of a trait represents the theoretical upper bound on variance explained by an optimal linear predictor (i.e., a polygenic score) constructed from the measured SNPs. In finite samples the realized out-of-sample R² of any PGS is therefore strictly lower than this bound, owing to estimation error in the SNP weights, imperfect LD tagging, and other sources of noise. Equality is attainable only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data. Hence the statement is correct.

12.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: False at first glance—PGS R2 can theoretically match SNP h2 under perfect tagging and infinite N, ~40%.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is jointly explained by all SNPs (i.e., \(\mathrm{Var}(G)/\mathrm{Var}(P)\), where \(G\) is the total additive genetic value tagged by the SNPs). A polygenic score is a single linear predictor \(\hat{G}=X\hat{\beta}\) whose weights \(\hat{\beta}\) are estimated from finite data. Because estimation error in \(\hat{\beta}\) is unavoidable, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{G})<\mathrm{Var}(G)\) and therefore \(R^2_{PGS}<h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples and optimal (BLUP) weights; under all practical conditions the inequality is strict. Hence the predictive ability of any realizable PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

(The statement remains true even for “all-SNP” scores; any shrinkage or pruning step further reduces attainable \(R^2\).)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance jointly explained by all measured (or tagged) variants; it is therefore the theoretical upper bound on out-of-sample prediction \(R^2\) that any polygenic score can achieve. With infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD tagging, and correctly specified additive effects, the polygenic score recovers exactly this quantity, so its predictive \(R^2\) equals—not is necessarily lower than—\(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the realized \(R^2\) is smaller because of estimation error, but the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total fraction of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by all SNPs in the population (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable by any linear combination of those SNPs). A polygenic score is a finite-sample estimate of the optimal weights; because of estimation error, incomplete LD tagging, winner’s-curse effects, and the need to apply shrinkage, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly less than this ceiling. Equality is reached only in the unattainable limit of infinite GWAS data, so in any real analysis the PGS variance explained is necessarily lower than \(h^2_{SNP}\).

(The statement is therefore True.)

A polygenic score is a linear predictor whose weights are estimated from finite data; because those weights contain sampling error, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the unattainable limit of infinite sample size and perfect LD. 11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by the additive effects of all measured (or imputed) SNPs. In the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size, perfect knowledge of linkage disequilibrium, and an identical ancestry distribution between discovery and target samples, a polygenic score constructed from the true SNP effect sizes will recover essentially all of that tagged variance; its out-of-sample \(R^2\) therefore approaches (but need not fall below) \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the realized \(R^2\) is lower because of estimation error, but the statement claims the inequality is *necessarily* strict—an assertion contradicted by the asymptotic result. Hence the claim is false.

(The practical gap between PGS \(R^2\) and \(h^2_{SNP}\) is usually large, yet that is an empirical observation, not a logical necessity.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by the SNPs (i.e., the variance of the true genetic value \(g\)). A polygenic score is a linear predictor \(\hat{g}\) whose weights are estimated from finite data; therefore its out-of-sample \(R^2\) equals \(h^2_{SNP} \times r^2(g,\hat{g})\). The correlation \(r(g,\hat{g})\) is strictly less than 1 whenever effect-size estimates contain sampling error, imperfect LD tagging, or population mismatch. Hence the inequality \(R^2_{PGS} < h^2_{SNP}\) necessarily holds in any real analysis. Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly matched data—an unattainable case under the usual definition of a polygenic score.

Final answer: True

A polygenic score (PGS), however, is constructed from finite-sample GWAS estimates of those effects; the resulting out-of-sample \(R^2\) is therefore attenuated by estimation error, incomplete LD tagging, winner’s-curse inflation, and possible differences in allele frequencies or environments between discovery and target cohorts. Consequently the attainable PGS \(R^2\) is bounded above by—and in any realistic setting strictly lower than—\(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is reached only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly matched samples, which never occurs in practice. Hence the statement is true.
